vtrmc-1990-01.title: Three linear equations
vtrmc-1990-01.body:
Let $g$ be the initial amount of grass per acre, $w$ the growth per acre per week, and $c$ the amount one cow eats per week. Eating a field bare means all the grass present (initial plus grown) is eaten:
$$\tfrac{10}{3}(g+4w)=12\cdot4c,\qquad 10(g+9w)=21\cdot9c,\qquad 24(g+18w)=n\cdot18c .$$
The first two give $g+4w=14.4c$ and $g+9w=18.9c$. Subtracting, $5w=4.5c$, so $w=0.9c$ and $g=14.4c-3.6c=10.8c$. Then
$$24(g+18w)=24(10.8c+16.2c)=24\cdot27c=648c=18nc\ \Rightarrow\ n=36 .$$

**Answer: 36 cows.**

vtrmc-1990-01.title: Per-acre reasoning
vtrmc-1990-01.body:
Work per acre. Field 1: $12$ cows on $\frac{10}3$ acres is $3.6$ cows per acre, eating an acre bare in $4$ weeks: $14.4$ cow-weeks per acre. Field 2: $2.1$ cows per acre for $9$ weeks: $18.9$ cow-weeks per acre.

The extra $5$ weeks supplied $18.9-14.4=4.5$ cow-weeks of grass per acre, so the grass grows $0.9$ cow-weeks per acre per week, and the initial grass is $14.4-4\cdot0.9=10.8$ cow-weeks per acre.

Over $18$ weeks an acre provides $10.8+18\cdot0.9=27$ cow-weeks, i.e. $\frac{27}{18}=1.5$ cows per acre. For $24$ acres: $24\cdot1.5=36$ cows.

**Answer: 36 cows.**

vtrmc-1990-02.title: Compare the sum with an integral
vtrmc-1990-02.body:
Counting the first join as the term $x=0$ (it takes $3=\frac{3\cdot1000}{1000}$ minutes), the total time in minutes is
$$N=\sum_{x=0}^{999}\frac{3(1000-x)}{1000+x}.$$
(Treating the first join separately and summing from $x=2$ changes $N$ by less than $3$ minutes.)

The function $\phi(x)=\frac{3(1000-x)}{1000+x}=-3+\frac{6000}{1000+x}$ is positive and decreasing on $[0,1000]$, so for each $x$, $\phi(x+1)\le\int_x^{x+1}\phi\le\phi(x)$. Summing over $x=0,\dots,999$:
$$N-3\le N-\phi(0)+\phi(1000)\le\int_0^{1000}\phi(x)\,dx\le N .$$
The integral is
$$\int_0^{1000}\Big(-3+\frac{6000}{1000+x}\Big)dx=-3000+6000\ln2=3000(2\ln2-1)\ \text{minutes}.$$
So $N$ is within $3$ minutes of $3000(2\ln2-1)$, and in hours
$$\frac N{60}\approx50(2\ln2-1).$$
With $\ln2\approx0.69$ this is $50\cdot0.38=19$ hours (with $\ln2=0.6931\ldots$: about $19.3$ hours).

**Answer: about $50(2\ln2-1)\approx19$ hours.**

vtrmc-1990-02.title: Trapezoid estimate
vtrmc-1990-02.body: A sharper estimate uses the trapezoid rule: $\sum_{x=0}^{999}\phi(x)\approx\int_0^{1000}\phi+\frac{\phi(0)-\phi(1000)}2=3000(2\ln2-1)+1.5$ minutes. Since $3000(2\ln2-1)\approx1158.9$ minutes, the puzzle takes about $1160$ minutes, i.e. $19.3$ hours. A direct computer summation gives $\approx1157$–$1160$ minutes depending on whether the first join is counted as $x=0$ or separately — in every reading about **19 hours**.

vtrmc-1990-03.title: Induction
vtrmc-1990-03.body:
Computing: $f(2)=f(f(1))+f(2-f(1))=f(1)+f(1)=2$, $f(3)=f(2)+f(1)=3$. We prove $f(n)=n$ for all $n\ge1$ by induction.

$f(1)=1$. Suppose $f(k)=k$ for all $k\le n$. Then
$$f(n+1)=f(f(n))+f(n+1-f(n))=f(n)+f(1)=n+1,$$
where we used $f(n)=n$ (so $f(f(n))=f(n)=n$, and $n+1-f(n)=1$). Hence $f(n)=n$ for all $n$.

(The recursion is well defined: whenever $f(1),\dots,f(n-1)$ equal $1,\dots,n-1$, the arguments $f(n-1)=n-1$ and $n-f(n-1)=1$ are already known, so $f$ is the unique function satisfying the rules.)

**Answer: $f(n)=n$.** ∎

vtrmc-1990-03.title: Verify the candidate and use uniqueness
vtrmc-1990-03.body: The identity function satisfies the rules: $f(1)=1$ and $f(f(n-1))+f(n-f(n-1))=(n-1)+(n-(n-1))=n$. On the other hand, the rules determine $f(n)$ from earlier values as long as the arguments $f(n-1)$ and $n-f(n-1)$ lie in $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$; by induction, if $f(k)=k$ for $k<n$, they are $n-1$ and $1$. So exactly one function satisfies the definition, namely $f(n)=n$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-04.title: Contradiction from the two equations
vtrmc-1990-04.body:
Write $P(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Z$, $a\ne0$, and suppose, for contradiction, that $a,b,c,d\ge-1$.

From $P(2)=0$: $8a+4b+2c+d=0$, so $d$ is even; since $d\ge-1$, $d\ge0$. Then
$$8a=-(4b+2c+d)\le-(-4-2+0)=6,$$
so $a\le0$; as $a\ne0$ and $a\ge-1$, $a=-1$. Now
$$4b+2c+d=8\qquad\text{and}\qquad b+c+d=1\ \ (\text{from }P(1)=0).$$
Subtracting four times the second from the first: $-2c-3d=4$, i.e. $-2c=4+3d\ge4$, so $c\le-2$ — contradicting $c\ge-1$.

Hence some coefficient is $\le-2$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-04.title: Factor out the known roots
vtrmc-1990-04.body:
Since $P(1)=P(2)=0$ and $P$ has degree $3$, $P(x)=(x-1)(x-2)(ax+e)=(x^2-3x+2)(ax+e)$, i.e.
$$P(x)=ax^3+(e-3a)x^2+(2a-3e)x+2e .$$
Here $a\ne0$ is an integer, and $e=(e-3a)+3a$ is an integer as well. Suppose all four coefficients are $\ge-1$. Then $2e\ge-1$ gives $e\ge0$, and $a\ge-1$.
- If $a\ge1$: $e-3a\ge-1$ gives $e\ge3a-1$, so $2a-3e\le2a-9a+3=3-7a\le-4$. Contradiction.
- If $a=-1$: $2a-3e=-2-3e\le-2$. Contradiction.

So some coefficient is $\le-2$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-05.title: Comparison and the $n$-th term test
vtrmc-1990-05.body:
**(a)** For $0<x\le1$ we have $\frac x2<\sin x<x$ (indeed $\sin x\ge x-\frac{x^3}6\ge\frac{5x}6$). So
$$\frac1{2n}<\sin\frac1n<\frac1n\qquad(n\ge1).$$
If $p\le0$, then $0<\sin\frac1n<1$ gives $\big(\sin\frac1n\big)^p\ge1$, so the terms do not tend to $0$ and the series diverges. If $p>0$, raising to the power $p$ gives
$$\frac{1}{2^p}\cdot\frac1{n^p}<\Big(\sin\frac1n\Big)^p<\frac1{n^p},$$
so by comparison with $\sum n^{-p}$ the series converges iff $p>1$. Altogether: **converges iff $p>1$**.

**(b)** Claim: $|\sin n|\ge\sin\frac12$ for at least one of any two consecutive integers $n,n+1$. Indeed, if $|\sin n|<\sin\frac12$, then $n$ lies within distance $\frac12$ of some multiple $k\pi$; then $n+1$ is at distance between $\frac12$ and $\frac32$ from $k\pi$ and at distance $>\pi-\frac32>\frac12$ from $(k\pm1)\pi$, so its distance $\delta$ to the nearest multiple of $\pi$ satisfies $\frac12\le\delta\le\frac\pi2$, giving $|\sin(n+1)|=\sin\delta\ge\sin\frac12$.

Hence infinitely many terms satisfy $|\sin n|^p\ge(\sin\frac12)^p>0$ when $p\ge0$; when $p<0$, every term is $\ge1$ (note $\sin n\ne0$ since $\pi$ is irrational). In all cases the terms do not tend to $0$, so the series **diverges for every $p$**. ∎

vtrmc-1990-05.title: Limit comparison for (a)
vtrmc-1990-05.body:
**(a)** Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\sin(1/n)}{1/n}=1$, we have $\lim\frac{(\sin1/n)^p}{n^{-p}}=1$ for every real $p$. Both series have positive terms, so by the limit comparison test $\sum(\sin\frac1n)^p$ converges iff $\sum n^{-p}$ does, i.e. iff $p>1$.

**(b)** As shown, $|\sin n|^p\not\to0$ (for $p>0$ infinitely many terms are $\ge(\sin\frac12)^p$; for $p\le0$ all terms are $\ge1$), so $\sum|\sin n|^p$ diverges for all real $p$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-06.title: Monotone and bounded
vtrmc-1990-06.body:
**(a)** $y^*$ is steady iff $y^*=y^*(2-y^*)$, i.e. $y^*(1-y^*)=0$: $y^*=0$ or $y^*=1$ (and conversely these stay fixed).

**(b)** Note $y_{n+1}=1-(1-y_n)^2$. If $0<y_n<1$, then $0<(1-y_n)^2<1$, so $0<y_{n+1}<1$; by induction $0<y_n<1$ for all $n$. Moreover
$$y_{n+1}-y_n=y_n(1-y_n)>0,$$
so $(y_n)$ is strictly increasing and bounded above by $1$; hence it converges to some $L\in(y_0,1]$. Passing to the limit in $y_{n+1}=y_n(2-y_n)$ gives $L=L(2-L)$, so $L\in\{0,1\}$, and $L\ge y_0>0$ forces $L=1$. Thus $y_n$ increases monotonically to the steady state $1$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-06.title: Explicit formula
vtrmc-1990-06.body:
Let $z_n=1-y_n$. Then $z_{n+1}=1-y_n(2-y_n)=(1-y_n)^2=z_n^2$, so
$$z_n=z_0^{2^n},\qquad y_n=1-(1-y_0)^{2^n}.$$
For $y_0\in(0,1)$, $0<1-y_0<1$, so $(1-y_0)^{2^n}$ decreases strictly to $0$. Hence $y_n$ increases strictly to $1$. Part (a) is also visible: $z$ is fixed iff $z^2=z$, i.e. $z\in\{0,1\}$, $y\in\{1,0\}$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-07.title: Divide by $1-f$
vtrmc-1990-07.body:
Take $A=-1$, $B=-1$, so that
$$F(x)=\frac{-g(x)}{f(x)-1}=\frac{g(x)}{1-f(x)} .$$
*Continuity.* By (ii), $1-f(x)\ge1-a>0$ on $[0,1]$, so $F$ is a quotient of continuous functions with nonvanishing denominator, hence continuous.

*Maximum.* By (iii), $g(x)+uf(x)\le u$ for all $x\in[0,1]$, i.e. $g(x)\le u\,(1-f(x))$. Dividing by $1-f(x)>0$: $F(x)\le u$ for all $x$. The maximum in (iii) is attained (continuous function on a compact interval) at some $y$, where $g(y)+uf(y)=u$, i.e. $F(y)=u$. Hence $\max_{[0,1]}F=u$. ∎

vtrmc-1990-07.title: How to guess $A$ and $B$
vtrmc-1990-07.body: At a point $y$ where the maximum in (iii) is attained, $g(y)=u(1-f(y))$, so $u=\frac{g(y)}{1-f(y)}$. This suggests $F=\frac{g}{1-f}$, i.e. $\frac{Ag}{f+B}$ with $A=B=-1$. The proof in the first approach then shows that $F(x)\le u$ everywhere with equality at $y$. (The choice is forced if $A,B$ are to work for all admissible data: with $g\equiv\frac12$, $f\equiv\frac12$, $u=1$ we need $\frac{A/2}{1/2+B}=1$, and with $g\equiv\frac34,f\equiv\frac14,u=1$ we need $\frac{3A/4}{1/4+B}=1$; together these give $A=B=-1$.) ∎

vtrmc-1990-08.title: Count the edges across a cut
vtrmc-1990-08.body:
We read the framework as the complete graph on the ten vertices (segments meet only at their endpoints), and removing a point from the interior of a segment cuts that segment. ("Vertex of $f$" in the statement means vertex of $F$.)

Suppose that after removing $8$ interior points the framework falls into two disjoint nonempty parts. Each remaining piece of a cut segment stays attached to one of its endpoints, so every vertex lies in one of the parts, and each part contains at least one vertex (a piece of a segment always contains an endpoint). Let the parts contain $k$ and $10-k$ vertices, $1\le k\le9$. Every one of the $k(10-k)$ segments joining a vertex of the first part to one of the second must have been cut — an uncut such segment would connect the two parts. Each removed point lies on one segment, so at least $k(10-k)$ points were removed. But
$$k(10-k)\ge1\cdot9=9\qquad(1\le k\le9),$$
since $k(10-k)-9=(k-1)(9-k)\ge0$. This contradicts the removal of only $8$ points. ∎

(For $k=1$ the bound $9$ is attained — this is the disconnection described in the statement.)

vtrmc-1990-08.title: Edge connectivity of $K_{10}$
vtrmc-1990-08.body: Equivalently, we must show that deleting $8$ edges from the complete graph $K_{10}$ leaves it connected. Take any two vertices $v,w$. If the edge $vw$ survives, they are connected. Otherwise, consider the $8$ paths $v\!-\!x\!-\!w$ through the other $8$ vertices $x$; these paths are edge-disjoint and disjoint from $vw$. At most $8-1=7$ further edges were deleted (one deletion was $vw$), so at least one of the $8$ paths survives intact. Hence any two vertices remain connected, and $F$ is not disconnected. ∎
